title: Refocusing Mammalian Synbio to Speak the Language of Biology (and Improve Human Health)
speaker: Ron Weiss
content: Synthetic biology is revolutionizing how we conceptualize and approach the engineering of biological systems. Recent advances in the field are allowing us to expand beyond the construction and analysis of small gene networks towards the implementation of complex multicellular systems with a variety of applications. In this talk I will describe our integrated computational / experimental approach to engineering complex behavior in a variety of cells, with a focus on mammalian cells. In our research, we appropriate design principles from electrical engineering and other established fields.
rawEventDetails: Speaker Ron Weiss Affiliation Massachusetts Institute of Technology Details Event Description Synthetic biology is revolutionizing how we conceptualize and approach the engineering of biological systems. Recent advances in the field are allowing us to expand beyond the construction and analysis of small gene networks towards the implementation of complex multicellular systems with a variety of applications. In this talk I will describe our integrated computational / experimental approach to engineering complex behavior in a variety of cells, with a focus on mammalian cells. In our research, we appropriate design principles from electrical engineering and other established fields. These principles include abstraction, standardization, modularity, and computer aided design. But we also spend considerable effort towards understanding what makes synthetic biology different from all other existing engineering disciplines and discovering new design and construction rules that are effective for this unique discipline. We will briefly describe the implementation of genetic circuits and modules with finely-tuned digital, analog, and multicellular behavior. We will also discuss the generation of a complex tissue from human induced pluripotent stem cells that recapitulates early developmental processes and exhibits a liver bud-like phenotype with integrated vasculature that can be used for drug development and potentially for tissue transplantation. Finally, we will present a mechanism for creation of artificial neural networks that operate in cells using translational regulation, providing a finely tuned mechanism for obtaining non-binary, non-monotonic behaviors with precise amplitude and temporal dynamics and paving the way for cells that can be trained and autonomously learn to perform specific behavioral tasks. Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar. Sponsor Omenn Darling Bioengineering Institute

rawEventDetails: Speaker Mattia Serra Affiliation University of California, San Diego Details Event Description Embryonic tissues undergo coordinated flows during avian gastrulation to establish the body plan. Here, we elucidate how tens of thousands of cells coordinate their behaviors to sculpt the chick embryo’s dynamic geometry (size and shape). Each of these two distinct geometric changes is associated with dynamic curves across which trajectories separate (kinematic repellers). Through physical modeling and experimental manipulations, we selectively eliminate either or both repellers in model and experiments, revealing their mechanistic origins. We find that embryo size is affected by the competition between extraembryonic epiboly and embryonic myosin-driven contraction—which persists even when mesoderm induction is blocked. Instead, the characteristic shape change from circular to pear-shaped arises from myosin-driven cell intercalations in the mesendoderm, irrespective of epiboly. These findings elucidate modular mechanisms that independently regulate embryo size and shape during development. Refreshments available 15 minutes before indicated time of seminar

speaker: Aditya Raguram

rawEventDetails: Speaker Aditya Raguram Affiliation Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research Details Event Description The ability to deliver proteins and RNAs into cells within the body is required for many emerging therapeutic modalities, including gene editing therapies, but efficient intracellular macromolecular delivery remains challenging. To address this challenge, we developed engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs): intracellular delivery vehicles that use retroviral scaffold proteins to package and deliver cargo proteins or RNAs instead of viral genetic material. We used protein engineering and capsid evolution to generate eVLPs that mediate highly efficient gene editing in mice and primary human cells. Additionally, we developed a genome-wide screening approach to systematically investigate how genetic perturbations in producer cells influence eVLP production, and we used this approach to engineer producer cells that support improved particle production and cargo delivery. Overall, eVLPs combine key advantages of both viral and non-viral delivery strategies and are promising tools for therapeutic gene editing, functional genomics, and disease modeling. title: Extensive Gene Evolution on Laboratory Timescales
speaker: Chang Liu
content: My group engineers genetic systems that accelerate the speed of gene evolution in vivo, enabling us to discover new biomolecular functions and explore sequence-to-function relationships at scale. I will summarize our development of orthogonal DNA replication (OrthoRep) to drive experimental evolution of chosen genes at 1-million times the genomic error rate. I will present applications OrthoRep to studying and engineering enzymes, antibodies, and arbitrary genes.Refreshments will be available 15 minutes prior to the start of the seminar.
